headline: The host's own CA bundle becomes trust anchors, and says which set you got.
summary: The toolkit read three published trust-store formats and none of them was the store the host is configured with, so validating against what a machine actually trusts meant exporting it by hand. `pki.trust.systemAnchors` reads the host's CA bundle into the anchors `pki.path.validate` consumes. It names which set it read, because the Mozilla set compiled into Node is not the host store, and an operator told otherwise would believe an internal root is trusted when it is not.

Added: `pki.trust.systemAnchors(opts?)` returns `{ anchors, source, path, skipped }`. `source` is `"ca-bundle"` for a file on this host, with `path` naming it, or `"node-bundled"` for the Mozilla set compiled into Node, whose `path` is `null`. The anchors are the same shape `parseCertdata` and `parseCcadbCsv` produce, so they reach `pki.path.validate` without being mapped by hand. `opts.path` reads a named file, `opts.maxBytes` caps the read.

The searched locations are the bundles a Unix host keeps: `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`, `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt`, `/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem`, `/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem`, `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` and `/usr/local/share/certs/ca-root-nss.crt`. Each candidate is tried by reading it, so one that exists but cannot be opened does not strand a readable one below it.

`pki.trust.discoversBundles(platform)` says whether that search runs. It does not on macOS or Windows: `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` can exist on macOS as OpenSSL's own copy, and returning it would report anchors that omit both locally installed roots and the Keychain trust decisions the host actually applies. Those platforms are refused instead, and `opts.path` still reads an exported bundle anywhere.

A host with no readable bundle is refused with `trust/no-readable-store`, and the message names the command that exports its roots. macOS keeps them in a binary keychain and Windows in a registry-backed store; reading either means running another program, which this toolkit does not do. `opts.allowNodeBundle: true` returns Node's set instead, reported as `"node-bundled"` so the difference is visible.

A block the bundle carries that is not a certificate, and a certificate the strict reader refuses, are both listed in `skipped` with the label, the byte offset and the reason. A CA bundle is distribution-managed and carries certificates that do not conform: the set Node ships has a root whose validity dates are before 2050 and encoded as GeneralizedTime, which RFC 5280 section 4.1.2.5 requires to be UTCTime. Refusing the whole file over one such root would leave you with no anchors, so it is named instead. A bundle from which no certificate parsed is still refused. A `BEGIN` boundary that does not start its line is reported too: RFC 7468 section 2 reads it as text rather than as a block, which in a trust bundle is an anchor you believe you installed and do not have.

An OpenSSL `TRUSTED CERTIFICATE` block is reported rather than ingested. It carries the purposes the operator trusted the root FOR in a trailing `X509_CERT_AUX`, and reading the certificate while dropping that would turn a root restricted to one purpose into an unrestricted anchor. The reported reason names the conversion, `openssl x509 -in <file> -out <file>.pem`. Reading the auxiliary data and keeping its restrictions is not yet implemented.

`opts.maxBytes` bounds what is read rather than what is kept, so a bundle far above the cap is refused without being loaded. A bundle that exceeds it is refused even under `opts.allowNodeBundle`: the cap is a fault about the file you named, and a resource refusal must not quietly swap the trust set a validation runs against.
